value: electrically driven vapour-compression heat pump on the reverse Carnot cycle: an evaporator takes heat from a low-temperature source, a compressor raises the fluid's temperature, a condenser releases the heat at the sink, and an expansion valve restarts the cycle. Sources include outdoor air, river, lake and sea water, ground heat, industrial and residential waste heat, and sewage heat. In industrial use it replaces boilers in many processes
note: NO INDUSTRIAL COST IS RECORDED FROM E19, DELIBERATELY. Every cost figure in the brief is residential (Table 4, USD/kW by world region) or non-residential buildings (Table 5, USD per refrigeration ton for building air-conditioning). Neither is an industrial process heat pump, and the sector vocabulary has no residential or commercial sector to hold them, so they sit in the _regional-costs.csv sidecar rather than being carried onto this row as a proxy. The design doc's rule applies - do not fill a gap with a proxy without saying so - and the heat pump capex gap is therefore still open after E19.
p.8: 'heat pumps are a mature technology'. Commercialised for heat supply since the second half of the 20th century.

COEFFICIENT OF PERFORMANCE - useful thermal energy out per unit of energy in, so a value above 1 is normal and 3 to 6 is the brief's typical range. UNIT IS 'COP', NOT 'fraction': populate.py normalises fraction to %, which would render a COP of 4 as 400%. p.1 adds that today's best heat pumps reach 6 to 7, and that efficiency has improved by a factor of 2.5 over past decades. The smaller the lift between source and sink, the higher the COP - so a COP quoted without its source and sink temperatures is not comparable across applications.

STEAM. p.8: 'today's heat pumps can produce hot air up to a temperature of 120 degC and steam up to 165 degC, and replace boilers in many industrial processes'; p.2 gives the same 165 degC steam figure. NOTE THIS CROSSES THE DESIGN DOC'S TIER BOUNDARY: 165 degC is above the 150 degC low/medium line in section 2, so an industrial heat pump reaches into the medium-temperature band, which is what heat-pump_electricity_medium-temp needed a source for. Research is expected to push the operating temperature further.

Capacity: p.1 gives 1 kW to 10 MW across all applications; p.7 says modular units can be assembled to 10 MW with high operational reliability. Recorded on the generic industrial row only, not repeated on the tier variants.

value: industrial heat pump delivering heat directly rather than through steam - hot air for drying and similar low-temperature process duty

note: HOT AIR, as distinct from the 165 degC steam figure on heat-pump_electricity. p.8: 'today's heat pumps can produce hot air up to a temperature of 120 degC'. p.2 lists generation of heated air for drying among the newer applications. 120 degC sits inside the design doc's low-temperature band (< 150 degC), which is where this technology belongs.
the brief's general range; it gives no separate COP for direct hot-air duty. See the note on heat-pump_electricity.

value: industrial heat pump raising steam into the medium-temperature band, up to 165 degC

note: E19 DISAGREES WITH THE ROSTER'S EXISTING TRL HERE, and the disagreement is worth keeping. The design doc section 4.3 carries this technology at TRL 6 on IEA's pulp-and-paper assessment, which reads as pre-commercial. E19 p.8 says in the present tense that 'today's heat pumps can produce ... steam up to 165 degC, and replace boilers in many industrial processes'. Either IEA is scoring a narrower duty than 165 degC steam, or the two sources are five years apart and the technology moved. No TRL is asserted from E19 - the state-of-development is recorded and the conflict left visible rather than resolved by picking a winner.

the top of the range E19 claims for industrial steam, and the reason this technology has a source at all. 165 degC is 15 degC above the design doc's 150 degC low/medium boundary, so this sits at the very bottom of the medium-temperature band and nowhere near its 400 degC ceiling.
the brief's general range. It gives no COP specific to 165 degC steam duty, and the COP falls as the lift rises, so the top of this range almost certainly does not apply at 165 degC.

value: centrifugal chiller - among the most efficient heat pump devices in the brief. Combined with thermal storage it cuts peak power; inverters cut consumption at low load
